questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] keeping a web app alive at 10x load (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/14). A ticketing app normally sees a steady trickle of buyers; a ticket drop sends 200 buyers at the same tier within seconds. Checkout calls a payment provider whose p50 is about 1.5 s, every route shares one database pool of 5 connections, door check-in and provider webhooks must keep working during the drop, and order expiry and QR generation run as jobs on a Redis-backed queue. Write your design before you look: who gets admitted and what a refusal looks like, the timeout on each hop, where retries live, how a slow dependency is kept from taking everything down, how the queue is operated, how the hot inventory row is handled, and how you would prove it under load. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Admission is decided before any scarce resource is taken, with limits per identity and per route rather than one global limit that would also throttle webhooks and door scanners; refused callers get a 429 with Retry-After or a waiting room.
keyPoints.quote: never one global limit that also blocks webhooks and scanners

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every outbound call has an explicit timeout shorter than its caller's, because library defaults are wrong for a request path (for example, the commonly cited Stripe SDK default of 80 s or Anthropic SDK default of 10 min, or a Redis client configured to retry forever).
keyPoints.quote: set shorter than the caller's timeout

keyPoints.text: [w3] Retries happen for idempotent work only, with exponential backoff plus jitter and a small cap, at exactly one layer, because stacked layers multiply (SDK x app x queue = 18 attempts).
[w3] The payment provider gets its own pool or concurrency limit (a bulkhead) and is called outside the database transaction, so slow payments cannot hold the connections check-in needs.
keyPoints.quote: so slow Stripe calls can't eat the connections that check-in needs

keyPoints.text: [w2] The hot tier row is decremented by one atomic conditional UPDATE guarded on remaining stock, no other step of a reservation contends on shared state (a single counter, a whole-table read), and Serializable is avoided where it only produces retries.
keyPoints.quote: avoid Serializable where it only yields retries

keyPoints.text: [w2] An in-process admission cap sits below the pool size, and pool or serialization errors that still escape map to 503 with Retry-After as the safety net.
keyPoints.quote: an in-process admission cap below the pool size

keyPoints.text: [w2] The job queue runs with worker concurrency sized to throughput, an alert on how long the oldest job has waited, and a Redis eviction policy that never evicts queue keys.
keyPoints.quote: never run BullMQ on a Redis with

keyPoints.text: [w1] The load test is shaped like the real event (a spike, not a ramp), passes or fails on an SLO, warms up first, and compares only with a baseline taken on the same machine.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — drop day, on a build whose checkout reserves stock inside a Serializable transaction with a version-checked update and an app-level retry loop: the payment provider slows down, a PR 'fixes' the resulting 500s by retrying 20 times with a fixed delay, Redis fills up, and a long generation job outlives its queue timeout. What breaks first, how does it show, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A provider call made inside a database transaction holds a pool connection for the provider's whole latency, so pool-timeout errors appear on unrelated routes, check-in included; an error that names a shared resource instead of a route is the tell.
keyPoints.quote: Look for errors that name a shared resource rather than a route

keyPoints.text: [w3] Retrying conflicts without jitter makes each retry a fresh conflicting transaction: attempts per success climb with concurrency, callers queue for connections until the pool wait times out, and latency gets much worse while most buyers still fail (in the lab, p95 went from 3.6 s to 14.3 s).
keyPoints.quote: Attempts per success grow with concurrency

keyPoints.text: [w2] The isolation level decides which error surfaces: at Serializable the version check aborts with an error the retry loop does not catch, so the designed optimistic-lock path never runs.
keyPoints.quote: Isolation level changes the failure mode, not just the speed.

keyPoints.text: [w2] With an LRU eviction policy, Redis under memory pressure can evict the queue's own repeatable-job schedule, so expiry jobs silently stop running.
keyPoints.quote: Redis eviction killed the expiry-job schedule

keyPoints.text: [w3] A queue timeout does not stop the handler: the job is retried while the first run is still going, so the handler needs a cancellation signal plumbed in (4 runs, 2 at once, for one job).
keyPoints.quote: the queue timeout is not a kill switch

keyPoints.text: [w2] Any hop still on a library-default timeout (or a Redis client that retries forever) waits as long as the slowing provider does, so the slowdown turns into held connections and busy workers instead of fast failures; it shows as latency on every route tracking the provider's latency.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your choices against the alternatives the chapter names: refusing fast vs letting callers wait in a queue, one retry layer vs retries everywhere, Serializable-plus-retry vs a single conditional update, and one shared pool vs per-dependency bulkheads. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] The wait bound must fit the refusal/latency budget: a refusal is only cheap if it is fast, and every second a caller waits in a queue before being told no is latency spent on the refusal, so a queue wait longer than the refusal target turns a correct 503 into a missed SLO.
keyPoints.quote: the 503s arrived after the 5 s queue wait

keyPoints.text: [w3] Retries at one layer is a written policy: the layer that owns retries is chosen and the others are configured not to retry, trading some inner-layer resilience for a known worst-case attempt count.
keyPoints.quote: write the M4 policy that keeps retries at one layer

keyPoints.text: [w2] Serializable plus retries turns contention into aborts and more load; a single conditional statement lets the database referee the stock in one round trip.
keyPoints.quote: The M1 sealed answer recommends a single conditional

keyPoints.text: [w3] A shared pool is simpler but lets the slowest dependency set everyone's latency; bulkheads cost capacity planning per dependency and buy a deliberate answer to which routes degrade first.
keyPoints.quote: you can say which routes degrade first

keyPoints.text: [w2] The cost of the single conditional update: the tier is still one hot row that every buyer serializes on, so its lock caps that tier's throughput; sharding the counter buys throughput back at the price of stock that is no longer a single row to read and reconcile.
keyPoints.quote: hot rows (a per-event counter) serialize everything
